opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly I'm still working through it. When we first saw how clean that trend was, with the length of tasks models can complete at around 50% reliability doubling roughly every seven months, and maybe faster more recently, my reaction was surprise. These are messy, heterogeneous software and research tasks, and you'd expect a lot of noise. Instead you get something that looks a lot like a straight line on a log plot over several years.

That pushed me in a couple of directions on the economic modeling side. First, it made me more sympathetic to models that treat AI progress as fairly smooth and predictable at the level of aggregate capability, rather than models built around discrete breakthroughs. If something this regular falls out of a mix of scaling compute, algorithmic improvements and better post-training, then maybe the right abstraction really is a few underlying inputs growing exponentially, with capabilities tracking them.

Second, and this is where I'm more cautious, I've become more aware of how big the gap is between "time horizon on our benchmark tasks" and "economic value." Our tasks are relatively self-contained. They have clear success criteria, and they don't require much context about an organization or long-term coordination with other people. Real jobs are full of that stuff. So I don't think you can take the trend, extrapolate it to tasks that take a month of human time, and conclude that a large fraction of remote work gets automated on that date. There are real questions about how well time horizons on messy tasks track the clean benchmark numbers, about reliability at 80 or 95% versus 50%, and about the cost of running these agents.

Third, the trend makes the feedback-loop question feel more pressing. Many economic models of explosive growth depend on AI accelerating AI research itself. If time horizons keep doubling, at some point models can do multi-day or multi-week chunks of research engineering. Whether that speeds up the trend, or whether you hit compute bottlenecks first, seems to me like one of the most important open empirical questions. The smoothness so far doesn't tell us much about whether there's a kink coming.

So my overall update is that I take quantitative forecasting more seriously than I used to, and the time-horizon lens has been a surprisingly useful way to think about it. But I'm also more humble about the step from a capability metric to actual economic impact. That step is where most of the uncertainty is, and it's what I'd most like to see more measurement on, like uplift studies and field data on how these systems perform when people actually deploy them.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses compute bottlenecks and uncertainty about economic impact, but does not predict that economy-wide funding constraints will prevent scaling to larger AI data centers.

r002.rationale: The candidate uses the trend to discuss economic models, but also distinguishes benchmark task horizons from economic value; it does not say the trend is closer to an economic model than an ML benchmark model.

r003.rationale: The candidate suggests aggregate AI capability may be smooth and driven by underlying inputs, but does not connect that systematicity to the apparent contingency of individual labs’ decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the time horizon trend was something I didn't really expect to be as clean as it has turned out to be. When we first put out the METR time horizons work, my prior was that you'd see something pretty noisy, where some tasks get solved and others don't and the aggregate picture is messy. Instead you get this fairly smooth doubling, and it's held up across a bunch of updates and new model releases, with maybe some acceleration in the recent period. That regularity itself is informative, independent of exactly what the doubling time is.

In terms of economic models, I'd say it pushed me in a couple of directions. The first is that a lot of the standard ways of thinking about automation, like the task-based models where you have a bundle of tasks and you ask what fraction a machine can do, kind of assume that the frontier of what's automatable moves in a jumpy, domain-specific way. The time horizon framing suggests there's a more unified underlying variable, something like how long a model can stay coherent and keep making progress on a problem without a human stepping in. And if that variable is growing exponentially, then the share of human work that falls under it isn't growing linearly, because the distribution of task lengths in the real economy is itself very skewed. A lot of what people do is short tasks, and then there's a long tail of things that take weeks or months. So you'd expect a period where AI looks modestly useful, and then a period where it flips pretty quickly as the horizon crosses the bulk of that distribution.

The second thing, and I want to be careful here, is that I've become more skeptical of taking the benchmark number and plugging it straight into an economic model. The time horizon we measure is on tasks that are, by construction, well-specified, self-contained, and automatically checkable. Real jobs are mostly not like that. There's context you have to acquire, there are stakeholders, there's ambiguity about what success even means. So when I see a model with a multi-hour horizon on our suite, I don't think that means it can replace a worker who does multi-hour tasks. I think of it as more like a leading indicator, where the capability shows up on the clean version first and then there's a lag before it translates into messy real-world settings. The question I find most interesting right now is how long that lag is, and whether it's shrinking.

The third thing is about what drives the trend. If it were just compute scaling, you'd expect it to be pretty sensitive to the economics of training runs. But a lot of the recent gains look like they come from post-training, from reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, from better scaffolding and tool use. Those are much cheaper inputs, which means the trend is probably more robust to things like capital constraints than a naive compute-centric model would predict. That's updated me toward thinking the capability side is less likely to be the bottleneck and the diffusion side, the organizational and integration stuff, is more likely to be where the action is in the near term.

So the honest summary is that the trend made me take the fast scenarios more seriously as a live possibility, but it also made me more attentive to the gap between measured capability and economically realized capability. I think a lot of the disagreement between people who look at these curves and say "transformative impact in a few years" and people who look at productivity statistics and say "where is it" comes down to that gap, and I don't think either side has a very good model of it yet.

r001.rationale: The response mentions capital constraints but says recent gains may be less sensitive to them; it does not predict funding constraints will eventually prevent larger data centers.

r002.rationale: It treats the trend as informative for economic models and discusses its economic implications, but does not say the trend is closer to an economic model than an ML benchmark model.

r003.rationale: It describes the smooth doubling trend as informative and suggests a unified underlying variable, but does not connect this systematicity to the apparent contingency of individual labs’ decisions.

astra-6.text:
It’s made me take models with fairly rapid transitions more seriously. You can imagine AI improving steadily on benchmarks while its economic impact grows quite slowly, because there’s always some part of a job it can’t do. But if the length of tasks it can reliably complete keeps increasing at a fairly consistent rate, that gives you a mechanism for moving from automating little pieces of work to automating much larger chunks.

The distinction I’d make is between that trend and the economic conclusions you draw from it. A task that takes a human several hours isn’t necessarily representative of several hours of work in a business. There are questions about context, supervision, and how costly mistakes are. So I wouldn’t just extrapolate the curve and read off a date for automating the economy.

But it does put pressure on models where those remaining tasks act as bottlenecks for a very long time. You need some account of why the trend would stop, or why increasing autonomy wouldn’t translate into economically useful work. I think that’s shifted me toward expecting potentially faster changes, while still being quite uncertain about how capability translates into deployment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses faster economic change and uncertainty about deployment, but says nothing about funding constraints or AI data center scaling.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes task-horizon trends from economic conclusions and cautions against extrapolating them directly. It does not characterize the trend itself as closer to an economic model than an ML benchmark model.

r003.rationale: It describes a consistent increase in task length and its possible implications, but does not connect that trend to systematicity in AI progress or to the contingency of labs’ decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s made me put more weight on the duration of tasks that AI can reliably complete as a variable in those models. You can have a system that’s very impressive on individual questions, but if you have to intervene every few minutes, that limits how much work you can actually delegate to it. As that horizon gets longer, the economic implications could change quite a lot, even if the underlying improvement is fairly smooth.

But I’d distinguish that from saying we’ve established a robust trend in economic output. A task taking a human several hours doesn’t necessarily mean that automating it saves several hours in a real workplace. There’s context, there’s checking the result, there’s integration with everything else. So I think the trend gives us a useful constraint on models: they should explain what happens as increasingly long tasks become delegable. It doesn’t, by itself, tell us how quickly that turns into productivity growth or an acceleration of AI research.
